summary: Defines the Network Control Protocol for setting up and configuring IPX over PPP. It was a standards-track specification. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: When two machines connect with PPP, this memo is the set of questions they use to agree on how to carry Novell IPX traffic.

questions: what is ppp network control protocol
subtitle: How two ends of a PPP link agree on the settings for carrying Novell IPX traffic.

tldr.problem: PPP can carry many network protocols, but each one needs its own setup step. IPX, the protocol used in Novell NetWare, had no such step for PPP links.
tldr.mechanism: IPXCP reuses the LCP packet exchange and adds six configuration options, such as the IPX network number, node number, compression and routing protocol. Once IPXCP reaches the Opened state, IPX datagrams can flow.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1552 is now Historic. It also had to coexist with Novell's separate IPX-WAN setup method, which shaped much of the design.

today: RFC 1552 is Historic. The unit metadata lists no replacement RFC. It was published in December 1993 as a Standards Track document, and it relates to RFC 1548 (PPP), RFC 1551 (IPX over WAN media) and RFC 1553 (IPX header compression).

sections.title: Where IPXCP Fits in PPP
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) has three parts: a way to wrap datagrams from many protocols, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) that sets up and tests the link, and a family of Network Control Protocols that configure each network-layer protocol. IPXCP is the Network Control Protocol for IPX, which was originally used in Novell's NetWare products.

The order is fixed. Both ends first use LCP to configure and test the link. Then PPP sends IPXCP packets to choose and configure IPX. Once IPXCP reaches the Opened state, IPX datagrams can be sent. The link stays up until LCP or IPXCP packets close it, or until an external event such as an inactivity timer or an administrator closes it.
sections.eli5: First the two computers shake hands to make sure the line works. Then they use IPXCP to agree on the Novell details. Only after that do real messages go through.

sections.title: How IPXCP Works
sections.content:
IPXCP uses the same packet exchange mechanism as LCP and is exactly the same as LCP with a few exceptions. One IPXCP packet goes in the Information field of a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hex 802B. Only Codes 1 through 7 are used: Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject. Other Codes should be treated as unrecognized and answered with a Code-Reject.

IPXCP packets may not be exchanged until PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase, and early ones should be silently discarded. Because authentication and link quality checks may still be running, an implementation should be ready to wait for them before timing out, and should give up only after user intervention or a configurable time.

Actual IPX data uses a different Protocol value, hex 002B, with exactly one IPX packet per frame. Since there is no standard way to fragment IPX datagrams, a PPP link supporting IPX MUST allow at least 576 octets in the Information field.
sections.eli5: The two computers use the same kind of question-and-answer cards that they used to set up the line, but with their own set of questions. IPX letters and setup cards get different stamps so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Coexisting with IPX-WAN
sections.content:
Novell had a separate method, IPX-WAN, that does a similar job over wide area links. To PPP, IPX-WAN packets are just IPX packets. The RFC notes that Novell had implemented IPXCP without any Configuration Options and required IPX-WAN to finish even when everything was configured by hand, so those products could not interoperate with other IPXCP implementations lacking IPX-WAN.

To bridge the gap, the RFC defines Desired Parameters: values an implementation may need for proper operation, which depends on the implementation. An implementation that supports IPX-WAN SHOULD always reach Opened state, even when a Desired Parameter could not be negotiated, so IPX-WAN can finish the job. One that does not support IPX-WAN SHOULD NOT reach Opened in that case. IPX-WAN Timer Request packets MUST NOT be sent until IPXCP has Opened the link. If setup cannot complete when a Desired Parameter is unknown, the link SHOULD be terminated by default, though that MUST be configurable.
sections.eli5: Novell already had its own way of doing the same job. This memo lets the new way and the old way live together, so machines that only know one still get along.

sections.title: The Six Configuration Options
sections.content:
IPXCP uses the LCP option format with its own set of options. If an option is missing from a Configure-Request, its default is assumed.

  • IPX-Network-Number (type 1, length 6): a four-octet network number. Both ends MUST have the same one, and it MUST be unique in the routing domain, or zero if unused for routing. A lower number in a request gets a Configure-Nak with the highest number.
  • IPX-Node-Number (type 2, length 8): a six-octet node number, which MUST be unique for the network number. Zero in a request asks the peer to supply a value.
  • IPX-Compression-Protocol (type 3): picks a compression protocol. Compression is off by default. Values include 0002 for Telebit Compressed IPX and 0235 for Shiva Compressed NCP/IPX.
  • IPX-Routing-Protocol (type 4): asks for a routing protocol. Values: 0 no routing protocol required, 2 Novell RIP/SAP, 4 Novell NLSP. RIP and SAP together are the default.
  • IPX-Router-Name (type 5): an advisory name of 1 to 47 characters, equivalent to the file server name on NetWare 3.x servers.
  • IPX-Configuration-Complete (type 6, length 2): advisory signal that all Desired Parameters are satisfied, which lets peers detect early whether setup will succeed.
sections.eli5: There are six questions: what is your network number, what is your own number, do we squeeze messages, how do we share maps, what is your name, and are you all set. The last one just says all done.

sections.title: Link Delay Guidance
sections.content:
The appendix addresses how to estimate link delay, which Novell routing protocols count in 55 millisecond ticks. IPX-WAN measures it with its Timer Request and Reply and multiplies the result by a factor of 6, since the measurement happens at link start-up and misses real load.

The RFC suggests measuring with the PPP LCP Echo facility instead, putting a timestamp in the request data and comparing it when the reply returns, with an echo size of 576 to match the default IPX packet size. Without dynamic measurement, it gives these empirical values: 2,400 bps is 134 ticks, 14,400 bps is 21 ticks, 57,600 bps is 5 ticks, and above 1 Mbps is 1 tick.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: Slow lines make messages take longer, so Novell counts delay in small ticks. A slower line gets a bigger tick count, and the memo gives a handy cheat table.

items.label: IPX-Network-Number
items.desc: Four-octet network number for the link.

items.label: IPX-Node-Number
items.desc: Six-octet node number for the local end.

items.label: IPX-Compression-Protocol
items.desc: Which compression protocol the sender can receive.

items.label: IPX-Routing-Protocol
items.desc: Which routing protocol the sender wants.

items.desc: Advisory name of the IPX entity.
